Deathtrap Schools

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The collapse of a walkway at Driehoek Hoerskool killed four children. But how safe are the rest of our public schools?

Unique Selling Point:
A broader look at the problem of crumbling, dilapidated infrastructure in our schools and the risk posed to learners and staff. We go to Driehoek Hoerskool to find out what went wrong, how it has affected the families of the deceased and the school family at large.
Who is responsible for the tragedy? What could have been done to prevent it? Who is liable for the loss of life and injury?


Summary:
We visit Ennerdale Secondary School south of Lenasia that identified structural problems two years ago. A walkway similar to the one that collapse at Driehoek Hoerskool has been propped up by scaffolding, and the building is out of bounds. Only the matric class is being catered for at the moment. They have had no response from the Department of Education about their issues, and this week staged a protest of 150 parents and staff who traveled to Pretoria to see the Minister of Education.

Further information:
SAOU gives details of more than 70 schools nationwide with infrastructure problems that pose a danger to learners. One of these, Roodepoort Hoerskool has closed off more than 18 classrooms because of their dilapidated condition. Storerooms and foyers have been turned into makeshift classrooms, while the school waits for the GDE to take action.

Who is responsible for identifying structural problems in schools? How often should schools be inspected? Who is responsible for fixing these problems? Who pays?

Press Release:


Death-trap Schools
The collapse of a walkway at Driehoek Hoërskool in Gauteng, killed four children leaving a community of parents, children and teachers, devastated. Now a new report shows that more than 70 public schools nationwide have infrastructure problems that could pose a danger to learners. Carte Blanche asks: how safe are children and teachers inside these hallowed halls of learning?
Producer: Kate Barry
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


DEATHTRAP SCHOOLS

V/O: There are over 24 000 public schools in South Africa, but with deteriorating buildings, how safe are our children? On the 1st of February the community of Van der Bijl Park was devastated by an accident at Hoerskool Driehoek.

Link: No-one could have been prepared for what happened that day. It was a normal school day after assembly, when this structure collapsed, killing 3 children immediately, and injuring several others.

Jacques: After assembly, the matrics would come out there, on top of the gallery in the hall. The matrics would come out there and they would walk this way to their classes. All the juniors would come out at this side of the hall, and then would get their suitcases which would be lying around here.

Clari: The next moment I woke up I was under the bridge, with my face against the ground.

V/O: Clari Botes is in Grade 12. She and her classmates were on top of an 8-ton concrete block which fell to the ground crushing the children below.

Clari: Once the block hit the ground, there was some sort of white flash or something. But the screams were very loud and haunting, mentally haunting.

Donovan: I just saw lots of kids on the grass, quite distraught.

V/O: Car salesman Donovan Olckers had two sons at Driehoek: Vincent in Grade 8 and Roydon in matric. He took Vincent home, before returning to look for Roydon.

Donovan: One guy told me he’s under the rubble, but he is okay and he is breathing, and he’s got a heartbeat. Even then I thought great, he's under there, but he's all right, he’ll make it. A certain police officer who we knew was looking for me, and he just walked to me and he said “Skuus Boeta, Royden is dood.” And, I went off my rocker. I just shouted No, no, no! I um, I asked him look I don't look at my son if he's in a bad physical state. But when I looked down I could clearly see his feet and his socks, where he was lying almost in a foetal position, and I could see quite a lot of blood around his top area shall we say.

V/O: Royden reportedly saved the lives of two young girls by pushing them out of the way of the falling block.

Mac: How would you describe him, what sort of a boy was he?

Donovan: He was a Christian boy, no was not perfect. But he really tried to be an example, he tried to spread love.

V/O: 17 year-old Royden, and two 13 year-olds - Marli Currie and Jandre Steyn – died at the scene, while 16 year-old Marnus Nagel died in hospital two days later. Twenty-two children sustained serious injuries, and four critically injured learners were airlifted to various hospitals. Clari spent 3 weeks in ICU at Milpark, before being transferred to the Netcare Rehabilitation Hospital.
Her father Pieter Botes knows there’s a long road to recovery.

Pieter: Her pelvis is broken in four places in front, two on the left, two on the right. Her leg was broken on one place, her leg was actually turned 180 degrees, and then her ankle was broken, and the ball of her foot was broken as well. And then her bladder had burst, and the liver had torn as well, so she had internal bleeding as well.

Mac: You’ve got private medical aid, but will it be enough to cover all your expenses?

Pieter: No, no it’s not. We received one invoice from the specialist who did the operations and the cost was 46 000 ad some change. The medical aid paid 12 100 and some change. It’s only one account from one doctor.

V/O: But over R2 million has been donated to assist the injured children. School Governing Body chairperson, Jacques Marx, is a trustee of the fund.

Mac: Do we know what caused the walkway to collapse?

Jacques: The official report hasn’t been released yet by the Department. It looks like just a freak accident at the moment.

Mac: Was there ever a time or an indication that that walk-way needed maintenance?

Jacques: No, not as far as I know and not as far as the Headmaster knows. There was no sign that anything was wrong at any moment in time before it actually happened, no.

V/O: The Gauteng Education Department is still waiting for several expert reports, according to MEC Panyaza Lesufi.

MEC: I’m waiting for all the reports, because I really believe let’s give the full picture. But I don’t think there’s nothing to hide. You just have to make these reports public. This has been a national issue, so when those reports are finalized I will personally release them.

V/O: It appears that the concrete block rested on four steel plates at each corner, supported by an angle iron, attached to the supporting poles. It is speculated that when rust caused one corner to fail, the others also gave way.

Mac: As an engineering technician, what do you think might have gone wrong there?

Pieter: I think there is a design problem. Obviously, with the photos of the rust, I think there is a maintenance problem as well.



Paul: The State as the owner of the property should be responsible for the infrastructural integrity of the building, and your School Governing Body for your day-to-day maintenance.

V/O: Paul Colditz is an education law specialist, and the CEO of FEDSAS, the federation of school governing bodies.

Mac: Who is responsible for identifying serious structural problems?

Paul: It would be the responsibility of the school governing body and the Principal. They’re on the property, you won’t have state officials walking around inspecting buildings. It can happen, but it doesn’t happen. So in the majority of cases the school governing body would inspect the buildings, and then report it to the Department of Education.

V/O: A national survey by the Suid Afrikaanse Onderwysers Unie, revealed that more than 70 schools have dangerous infrastructure, including dilapidated roofs, corridors, cracked walls, staircases and asbestos classrooms. 68% of the infrastructure problems were reported to the Department of Basic Education, but 71% of the schools did not receive any feedback. Ennerdale Secondary School has been waiting 5 years for repairs.

MEC: It takes time. People are impatient because they feel the school can fall anytime. And I have assured them that we are attending to your issue.

Jacobus: We’ve had these support structures here for the last three-and-a-half to four years now. A few years ago one of the engineers cane out and declared the fact that we need to replace or fix these walkways. Nothing happened.

V/O: But after the Driehoek incident, they decided to take the matter further, according to Principal Jacobus Souls

Jacobus: That tragedy touched all of us. As teachers any child is our child.

V/O: Two weeks ago he led a delegation to the national Minister in Pretoria, who sent an engineer to inspect the school the next day.

Jacobus: He told us to declare it is a danger zone. It is the two walkways. It is this building, The building, that is that building, have been tilted already by about 10 mm.

Mac: That’s a disaster waiting to happen?

Jacobus: It is a disaster waiting to happen. And then, because of the fact that the toilets are attached to that walkway that side, that can’t also be utilized.

V/O: That means that 21 classrooms are off-limits, and only the matrics can be accommodated by the school.

Link: Fortunately there have been no serious incidents reported at Ennerdale Secondary School. However, due to the danger that these buildings pose, close to a thousand children are now at home and missing school.

MEC: I can mention others schools. Go to Roodepoort High School, it is the same situation. The old infrastructure - it’s sell-by date is coming to an end at a very fast pace that doesn’t match the financial allocations that we receive as a sector.

V/O: Eighteen classrooms at Hoerskool Roodepoort are closed, due to sagging floors and visible cracks in the walls. But perhaps the most widespread danger in South African schools are pit latrines, which claimed the lives of 5-year olds, Lumka Mkweta and Michael Komape.

Hopolang: We have about 24 000 public schools, 3 800 only have pit latrines. It’s not the majority, but it’s a significant number when you consider how dangerous they are. We’ve lost 2 learners that we know of in pit latrines.

V/O: Pit latrines are banned, but many schools in rural areas don’t meet the Minimum Uniform Norms and Standards, according to Hopolang Selebalo from the organization, Equal Education.

Hopolang: We found learners learning in mud schools. The walls are obviously fragile, they’re crumbling, rain comes in through the roof.

Paul: The State is liable for any loss or damage suffered by any person, not only the learners or teachers, that has occurred during a school activity. If the school has public liability insurance, the State will only cover those losses or damages not covered by the school’s liability insurance.

MEC: That is why you have to wait for the report, but if the report says we are responsible, we have to take the blame. Everything that happens within this schooling environment, whether good or bad, we must carry the burden. If we need to fall on our sword, we have to fall on our sword, why not?

V/O: Until then, learners at Hoerskool Driehoek are being taught in tents while they wait for the school buildings to be declared safe.
